stops.title: Read the rules, call the first number
stops.silver: Planning means someone hands you the rules of the world, where each move leads and what it pays, so the only job left is to work out what to do.
stops.do: The board is 25 pads on the floor, all showing 0, with the rules in the orange row on the left. Answer the question floating in front of you with LEFT CLICK, RIGHT CLICK or MELEE, then press F to run sweep 1.
stops.predict: After one sweep, what number will the pad right next to the goal show?
stops.saw: The three pads beside the goal jumped to 9 and every other pad to -1. In one sweep each pad looks one step ahead: the step costs 1, and only a pad next to the goal can see its 10. That one-step look ahead is lecture 2's Bellman rule, used here as an update because the rules are known in advance.
stops.agent: An agent that knows exactly what a tool returns can score a call before making it, the way a pad scores a move before taking it.

stops.title: Watch the good news spread
stops.silver: In his small gridworld the value of a square (the total reward you can expect from it) is found by sweeping over every square again and again, and the numbers fill in a little more each time.
stops.do: Answer the question, then press F for sweep 2 and watch which pads turn yellow.
stops.predict: On which sweep will your own start pad, the blue ring, first turn positive?
stops.saw: Yellow marks the pads that just heard about the goal: a new ring of them each sweep, one pad further out. Each pad reads only its neighbours' numbers from the sweep before, so news travels one step per sweep. Your start pad is 5 steps from the goal, so it turns positive on sweep 5, which you will see in stop 4.

stops.title: Judge a half-finished board
stops.silver: Value iteration (sweep, keep the best move's number, sweep again) ends at the best values, but a table halfway through need not be the score of any real plan.
stops.do: The board now shows sweep 2. Answer the question, then press F for sweep 3.
stops.predict: Is there one plan, one fixed choice of step on every pad, whose scores are exactly the numbers on the board right now?
stops.saw: No plan scores these numbers. A pad showing -2 whose neighbours all show -2 would score -3 under any plan, because every step costs 1 and lands on a -2. The midway numbers are unfinished sums: two steps of cost counted, the goal not yet seen. Only the settled table is the value of a plan.

stops.title: Sweep until nothing moves
stops.silver: In his shortest-path grid the far corner needed one sweep for every step of distance before its number was right, and the method stops once a whole sweep changes nothing.
stops.do: Answer the question, then keep pressing F, one sweep per press, until the panel on the right says 0 pads changed. Green lines then appear on the pads.
stops.predict: Which sweep will be the first that changes nothing at all?
stops.saw: The farthest pad got its final number on sweep 7, and sweep 8 changed nothing, which is the only way to know you are done. The green lines are the plan: on each pad, the step toward the best number next door. Choosing that way is called acting greedily, or policy improvement. Eight sweeps of 22 pads and 4 moves came to 704 look-aheads.

stops.title: Walk the plan yourself
stops.silver: His summary splits planning in two: prediction finds how good a given plan is, control finds the best plan, and every sweep costs each state times each move.
stops.do: Answer the question, then walk with WASD along the green lines from the blue ring to the green goal ring. Each pad you enter costs 1 and the goal pays 10.
stops.predict: Your start pad shows 5. If you follow the lines, what will you score?
stops.saw: Following the lines scores 5: five pads at -1 each, plus 10 at the goal. That is the start pad's number exactly, because a pad's number is what the plan earns from there. Checking what a plan earns is called policy evaluation. If you wandered off the lines, the score on the left came out lower than the pad said.
stops.agent: A score for a half-finished conversation, such as a reward model's, plays the same part as the pad's number, though nothing makes it this exact.

stops.title: Move a pit, then plan again
stops.silver: You need not sweep every state every time: updating single states, in a good order or first where the numbers would change most, still reaches the same answer.
stops.do: Walk to any pad and press R: the pit marked THIS PIT MOVES jumps there. Answer the question, then press F; the board is wiped and the sweeps run by themselves.
stops.predict: How many of the old green lines are no longer the best step once the pit has moved?
stops.saw: Only pads whose best route ran past the new pit change their minds, and their lines turn yellow. A pit on the pad just ahead of the start flips 5 lines; a pit where no best route passes flips none. The game wiped the board and swept all of it again, yet most settled numbers came back the same. Updating first the pads that would move most is what Silver calls prioritised sweeping.

stops.title: Read the debrief
stops.silver: Every update here used the full rules and every branch, which is costly and needs a model of the world, and later lectures learn from single real steps instead.
stops.do: Nothing to press. Read the three lines on the left: what you did, what it is called, and where it shows up in a language-model agent.
stops.predict: Could this planner have found the plan if nobody had told it where the pits were?
stops.saw: It could not. Every sweep read the rules: where each move lands and what it pays. Without them a player has to walk and fall to find out, which is what the learning methods from lecture 4 on do. The board was also tiny at 25 pads, where a real match has far too many states for even one sweep.
stops.agent: A language-model agent can think a tool call through only when it has a model of what the tool will do; without one it has to make the call and learn from the result.
